title: Transaction commit performs sequential unrolled mutations with no-op rollback
summary: FileObjectTransaction advertises multi-operation ACID transactional semantics, but commitStageApplyPerOpMixed executes mutations sequentially via direct tx.storage.Create and tx.storage.Update calls. When an intermediate operation fails (e.g. disk full, schema validation, membrane refusal), tx.Rollback(ctx) is called. However, Rollback is implemented as an explicit no-op ('tx.ops = nil') under the false assumption that mutations have not yet been applied. Prior operations in the transaction remain permanently committed to CAS/disk, violating atomicity and leaving repository state partially corrupted.
recommendation: Implement true all-or-nothing transactional atomicity. In commitStageApplyPerOpMixed, maintain a compensation journal of applied operations and systematically execute compensating inverse mutations (e.g. Delete for previously created objects, restore previous state for updated objects) upon failure before returning, or stage all mutations in an isolated scratch/staging directory before atomically swapping or linking them into place.

evidence.detail: Sequential per-op application loop invokes tx.Rollback(ctx) on intermediate Create/Update failure
Rollback implementation is an empty no-op clearing tx.ops with comment 'no-op for file backend since we haven't applied changes yet'

citations.point: Chapter 7: Transactions - Atomicity guarantees that if an error occurs during a multi-operation transaction, any writes that were already made must be discarded or undone (abortability).
Reliability - Fault tolerance: degree to which a system operates as intended despite the presence of hardware or software faults.

title: Darwin async fsync queue drops durability on immediate CLI command exit
summary: On macOS (Darwin), CasPublishSyncFileOS delegates file fsync to an unmonitored in-memory channel (darwinSyncQueue, capacity 1024) processed by a detached background goroutine to avoid F_FULLFSYNC latency during publication. However, the runtime provides zero drain mechanisms, shutdown hooks, or exit handlers. When any short-lived CLI command (e.g. zqk object create, zqk system init) creates a CAS object and exits (os.Exit(0)), the Go runtime abruptly terminates all background goroutines before dupFD.Sync() can execute. As a result, newly published CAS objects lack hardware-flush durability and are vulnerable to truncation or zeroing upon power loss or kernel panic.
recommendation: Provide an explicit, thread-safe Flush/Drain function for darwinSyncQueue and register it with the CLI shutdown lifecycle (e.g. cli.Processor termination or ShutdownManager). Ensure that synchronous CLI commands either await fsync completion or explicitly drain pending file sync operations before exiting.
non_goals: Re-introducing synchronous 10-minute F_FULLFSYNC stalls during heavy Time Machine or Spotlight runs

evidence.detail: Detached background goroutine reads darwinSyncQueue with no lifecycle termination or flush coordination
CasPublishSyncFileOS enqueues dupFD to darwinSyncQueue and returns nil immediately
WriteObject calls CasPublishSyncFile(tmp) and immediately links into CAS without verifying disk flush completion

citations.point: Chapter 3: Reliable storage engines require explicit fsync calls to force operating system write caches to flush to persistent disk before acknowledging completion.
Goroutines terminate abruptly when main or os.Exit finishes; background workers managing I/O resources must be coordinated via WaitGroups or explicit drain channels before process exit.

verification_proof: Remediated in codebase and verified under unit/race tests

title: Privileged Writer IPC client discards context and executes unbounded synchronous RPC
summary: The PrivilegedWriter IPC client (IPCWriter) connects to the helper daemon via net/rpc over a Unix domain socket. While WriteObject, DeleteObject, and RenameObject accept a ctx context.Context parameter, the context is completely ignored and discarded. The client invokes net/rpc.Client.Call synchronously with no timeout, deadline, or cancellation propagation. If the daemon deadlocks, becomes unresponsive, or blocks on file I/O, every CLI command and background agent attempting storage mutation hangs indefinitely with no timeout recovery.
recommendation: Propagate ctx to RPC calls using an asynchronous channel pattern (client.Go) paired with select on ctx.Done() and a configurable call timeout. Ensure connection establishment in NewIPCWriter enforces a bounded dial timeout rather than indefinite blocking.
non_goals: Replacing net/rpc with a heavyweight gRPC or HTTP/2 stack across the local Unix socket boundary

evidence.detail: rpc.Dial("unix", socketPath) executes with no connection timeout
ctx parameter is discarded; client executes blocking w.client.Call with no deadline
IPC server accepts connections without read/write timeouts or idle keepalive enforcement

citations.work: Google Site Reliability Engineering (Beyer et al.)
citations.point: Chapter 21: Addressing Cascading Failures - When a deadline is not specified for an RPC, clients will wait indefinitely for the server to reply. A system must propagate deadlines through all layers.
Client.Call is synchronous and does not respect Context. For context-aware cancellation, Client.Go must be combined with a select loop on <-call.Done and <-ctx.Done().

title: Write-behind worker drops mutations and advances checkpoints on save-queue full errors
summary: In object_write_behind_worker.go (processOneOrMore and drain), when apply returns an error matching isRetryableWriteBehindApplyDrop (ConstStreamSaveQueueIsFull, indicating HashRegistry saveQueue capacity exhaustion), the worker removes the pending op from the in-memory buffer (w.buf.RemoveFront) and flushes the checkpoint to disk (WriteAppliedSeq(op.Seq)). The comment asserts that '(WAL retains the op for replay)', but advancing applied_seq guarantees that subsequent startup replays and backlog sweeps will never replay this sequence. When CompactWAL executes, it permanently purges all WAL records where seq <= applied_seq, resulting in irrecoverable silent data loss.
recommendation: Never advance applied_seq for dropped or unpersisted mutations. When the HashRegistry queue is full, apply exponential backoff and pause write-behind processing until the queue drains, or quarantine the failed sequence to a dead-letter log before advancing checkpoints.
non_goals: Infinite in-memory queue growth without backpressure

evidence.detail: When isRetryableWriteBehindApplyDrop(err) is true, worker removes op from buffer and calls flushCheckpoint(pendingSeq)
Shutdown drain drops retryable errors and writes applied seq directly to checkpoint file
Identifies ConstStreamSaveQueueIsFull as a drop-and-advance error condition

citations.point: Chapter 3: Write-Ahead Logging - Checkpoint advancement must only reflect operations that have been durably applied to the underlying storage engine. Advancing checkpoints past uncommitted writes guarantees data loss.
Reliability - Recoverability: degree to which, in the event of an interruption or a failure, a product or system can recover the data directly affected and re-establish the desired state.

title: JobLock stale lock cleanup unlinks lock file breaking flock mutual exclusion
summary: JobLock implements distributed mutual exclusion for scheduler jobs across processes using POSIX flock. In NewJobLockWithConfig, NewFileLock opens lockPath and caches the open file descriptor. In Acquire() and TryAcquire(), checkAndCleanStaleLock() evaluates info.ModTime(). If age exceeds StaleLockThreshold (default 1h), it removes lockPath from disk via fileutil.Remove(). When fileLock.LockWithTimeout() then executes, it acquires flock on an unlinked inode. Concurrently, a second process calling NewJobLock creates and locks a brand new inode at the recreated lockPath. Both processes concurrently hold exclusive locks on different inodes, completely defeating mutual exclusion and allowing overlapping execution of singleton tasks.
recommendation: Never unlink an flock lock file to break stale locks. Instead, use non-blocking flock acquisition (unix.LOCK_NB) to verify whether another live process holds the lock; if flock succeeds, the lock is definitively not held regardless of file modification timestamp. If PID tracking is needed, record the owner PID in the file payload and check /proc or kill(pid, 0) before acquisition without unlinking the file.
non_goals: Replacing filesystem flock with an external distributed consensus engine like etcd or Consul

evidence.detail: File descriptor is opened during NewFileLock before stale lock check occurs
Acquire calls checkAndCleanStaleLock before invoking fileLock.LockWithTimeout
Removes lockPath when age > threshold while file descriptor was already opened on old inode

citations.point: flock locks are associated with the open file table entry (inode). Removing a locked file from the directory tree does not release the lock, but causes subsequent open calls to refer to a new, different file, breaking mutual exclusion.
Chapter 8: Distributed Locks and Fencing - Timeouts based on elapsed wall-clock time cannot safely determine lock ownership due to process pauses, garbage collection, and I/O stalls.
citations.locator: Chapter 8: The Truth Is Defined by the Majority

verification_proof: Remediated in codebase and verified under unit/race tests

title: WAL compaction silently purges corrupted log lines without quarantine
summary: During WAL replay (ReplayWALChunk) and compaction (CompactWAL), when parseWALLine encounters an invalid or torn record, it logs a warning and skips the line (continue). If any subsequent valid line is processed, applied_seq advances past the damaged entry. When CompactWAL executes, corrupted records are omitted from the compacted output file, and fileutil.Rename overwrites the original WAL. Damaged or corrupted transactions are permanently eradicated from disk without creating a quarantine copy (.corrupt or .quarantine), eliminating all auditability and post-mortem forensic recovery.
recommendation: When an unparseable or corrupted record is detected during compaction, halt compaction or archive the pre-compaction WAL file with a timestamped quarantine extension (e.g. object.wal.corrupt.<timestamp>) before performing an atomic rename. Introduce record-level CRC32/Adler32 checksums into the WAL format to distinguish torn tails from middle-of-file bit rot.
non_goals: Refusing to start up when encountering a torn tail at the EOF caused by an unbuffered crash

evidence.detail: Unparseable line in ReplayWALChunk is logged as warning and skipped without quarantine
CompactWAL skips unparseable line from unappliedRecords
Atomically overwrites original WAL file via fileutil.Rename without preserving corrupted records

citations.point: Chapter 3: Storage engines using write-ahead logs must employ checksums to detect corruption and must avoid silently discarding corrupted records without explicit administrative notification and salvage mechanisms.
Reliability - Recoverability: degree to which a product can recover data directly affected and maintain data integrity in the event of an interruption.

title: Worker pool task panic terminates worker goroutines causing pool starvation
summary: goroutinelabels.Pool provides a fixed-size worker pool (default size 10) for executing swarm tasks and background jobs. In pool.go, each worker goroutine runs a loop: for { select { case w := <-p.work: _ = w.fn(w.ctx) } }. Although the outer goroutine builder catches panics to invoke an optional onPanic callback, a panic within w.fn unwinds the entire worker goroutine, exiting the for loop permanently. The pool does not detect worker death or spawn replacement goroutines. If 10 tasks trigger an unhandled panic (e.g. nil pointer dereference during LLM parsing or prompt formatting), all 10 worker goroutines die, completely paralyzing the pool and permanently halting all subsequent task execution.
recommendation: Wrap the individual task invocation (_ = w.fn(w.ctx)) inside an inner defer/recover function within the worker loop. When a task panics, log the stack trace, record a failure metric, and continue the worker loop to service subsequent tasks.
non_goals: Allowing infinite unhandled panics without alerting operators

evidence.detail: Worker loop executes _ = w.fn(w.ctx) without inner recover block
Swarm tasks execute on a shared bounded pool of 10 workers

citations.point: Panic and Recover - Long-running server processes must protect worker goroutines from panics caused by individual requests, ensuring that a single failing request does not crash the server or worker thread.
Reliability - Availability: degree to which a system or component is operational and accessible when required for use.

verification_proof: Remediated in codebase and verified under unit/race tests

title: RelayServer cleanupLoop lacks shutdown lifecycle leaking background goroutines
summary: In pkg/relay/server.go, NewServer starts a background goroutine executing s.cleanupLoop() via goroutinelabels.NewGoroutine. The cleanupLoop runs an infinite ticker loop (for range ticker.C) with no context parameter, no stop channel, and no termination check. RelayServer exposes no Close() or Stop() method. Every initialization of RelayServer permanently leaks a background goroutine. Furthermore, BufferPayload appends incoming messages into s.buffers[clientID] without checking individual or aggregate slice capacity or memory boundaries, enabling unbounded memory exhaustion under disconnected client traffic.
recommendation: Add a context parameter or stop channel to RelayServer, pass it to cleanupLoop, and provide a Close() method that stops the ticker and waits for goroutine exit. Bound s.buffers with a maximum queue depth per client.
non_goals: Implementing an external persistent queue (e.g. Redis or Kafka) for sovereign relay

evidence.detail: NewServer spawns cleanupLoop in detached goroutine without passing context or stop channel
cleanupLoop executes infinite for range ticker.C with no exit condition
BufferPayload unconditionally appends payloads to slice with no size or count cap

citations.point: Goroutines must have a clear lifetime and clean shutdown mechanism to prevent resource leaks.
Resource Hygiene and Goroutine Lifecycle Safety: Goroutines must possess deterministic lifecycle ownership and termination signals.

title: Uncached object file reader truncates YAML data on partial stream read
summary: In pkg/storage/object_storage_file_helpers_read_impl.go, readObjectFileNoCache reads YAML files directly from disk to bypass OS caching. It allocates a buffer data = make([]byte, stat.Size()), calls n, err := file.Read(data), and slices data = data[:n]. Under POSIX and Go io.Reader semantics, Read is permitted to return fewer bytes than requested (n < stat.Size()) even when more data is available. Truncating to n without calling io.ReadFull causes incomplete YAML to be passed to the parser, triggering false syntax errors or corrupting deserialized objects during cache-bypass reads.
recommendation: Replace file.Read with io.ReadFull(file, data) or io.ReadAll(file) to guarantee that all file bytes are retrieved prior to parsing.

evidence.detail: Reads from file via single file.Read and slices data[:n] without io.ReadFull

citations.point: Read reads up to len(p) bytes into p. Callers should treat a return of 0 <= n <= len(p) as the number of bytes read; use io.ReadFull to read exactly len(p) bytes.
Standard I/O helpers like io.ReadAll or io.ReadFull should be preferred over raw Read calls when reading known-length buffers.

verification_proof: Remediated in codebase and verified under unit/race tests
